The claim appears supported: read() can fill all 64 bytes with non-NUL data, and strncmp/ALOGD %s would read past. But is there any in-function fact defeating it? No clamp on result, no forced NUL. retraction_cases.counterexample: Any successful key_alloc call where security_key_alloc returns < 0: key is allocated with kmem_cache_zalloc (line 53), so key->description is NULL; line 58 stores the kmemdup result in key->index_key.description, and line 98 frees key->description which is NULL, not a stale pointer.
retraction_cases.reason: The key struct is zero-allocated at line 53, so key->description is NULL and line 98 frees NULL rather than an uninitialized or stale pointer, defeating the 'freeing wrong/stale pointer' scenario. The claim's remaining leak scenario (index_key.description not freed) is not defeated by this fact, but the cited defect of freeing a stale pointer is concretely refuted.

retraction_cases.counterexample: fieldNames="a,b" with atts[i]="a,b": first key = estrndup(p1, p2-p1) allocates p2-p1+1 bytes and NUL-terminates, so add_assoc_zval_ex(ent.data, key, p2-p1+1, tmp) passes a length that exactly matches the allocated buffer including its NUL; the trailing segment uses p1..endp which is also NUL-terminated within the attribute string, so endp-p1+1 stays within bounds.
retraction_cases.reason: The cited lengths p2-p1+1 and endp-p1+1 are not reads past the buffer: estrndup at line 124 allocates exactly p2-p1+1 bytes (content plus NUL), and the final segment at line 135 spans p1 through endp inclusive, which is within the NUL-terminated attribute string. Thus the length including the NUL matches the available buffer and does not over-read.
